### Chapter 10: Risk Measures Beyond Variance {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
Re <- R - rf
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))

loss_es <- function(x) as.numeric(ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "historical", invert = FALSE))
w_of    <- function(opt) extractWeights(opt)[colnames(Re)]
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")
w_var <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                                 optimize_method = "ROI"))
```

#### Exercise 1

The level enters @eq-10-lp only through $\alpha$, so each solve is one line
apart from the last; the number of months in the tail is $\alpha T$.

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex1
min_es_at <- function(p) {
  spec <- base_spec |>
    add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES", arguments = list(p = p, method = "historical"))
  w <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec, optimize_method = "ROI"))
  tibble::tibble(p = p, tail_months = (1 - p) * nrow(Re),
                 US_credit = w[["US_credit"]],
                 largest = names(which.max(w)), largest_weight = max(w),
                 to_min_variance = sum(abs(w - w_var)) / 2)
}
ex1 <- dplyr::bind_rows(lapply(c(0.90, 0.95, 0.99), min_es_at))
ex1 |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))) |> as.data.frame()
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex1-facts
#| include: false
# What the answer states: no credit at any level, one largest holding, and a
# distance to minimum variance that grows with the level.
stopifnot(all(ex1$US_credit < 0.005), length(unique(ex1$largest)) == 1L,
          all(ex1$to_min_variance > 0), !is.unsorted(ex1$p), all(diff(ex1$to_min_variance) > 0))
```

`US_credit` is held at none of the three levels, and the largest holding is
`r paste0("\x60", unique(ex1$largest), "\x60")` at every one of
them. The last column is the share of the portfolio that would have to be
traded to reach the minimum-variance solution: it is
`r sprintf("%.3f", ex1$to_min_variance[ex1$p == 0.90])` at `p = 0.90`,
`r sprintf("%.3f", ex1$to_min_variance[ex1$p == 0.95])` at `p = 0.95` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", ex1$to_min_variance[ex1$p == 0.99])` at `p = 0.99`. The
solutions never coincide with the minimum-variance portfolio, and they move
away from it as the level rises, because what changes with `p` is the support
of the estimate. At `p = 0.99` the tail holds
`r sprintf("%.1f", ex1$tail_months[ex1$p == 0.99])` months, and @eq-10-lp then
chooses sixteen weights to make the average of three or four observations
as small as possible, which is a fit to those months rather than an estimate
of a tail; @yamai2005 give the standard error that grows as the tail
shrinks, and @sec-08-estimation-error-theory is about what an optimizer
does with such an input.

#### Exercise 2

The weekly returns are the model's native frequency and the monthly ones are
compounded from them, so the two panels describe the same sample with about
four times as many observations in every tail. The weekly bill starts one
week before the returns do and is matched by date.

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex2
#| warning: false
Rw  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_weekly, date, class, return)
rfw <- sim_riskfree_weekly$return[match(zoo::index(Rw), sim_riskfree_weekly$date)]
stopifnot(!anyNA(rfw), ncol(Rw) == 16L)
Rew <- Rw - rfw
spec_w <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Rew)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

credit_gap <- function(X, spec, n = 25) {
  fr_es <- as.data.frame(unclass(create.EfficientFrontier(X,
    spec |> add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
            add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES", arguments = list(p = 0.95)),
    type = "mean-ETL", n.portfolios = n, optimize_method = "ROI")$frontier))
  fr_sd <- as.data.frame(unclass(create.EfficientFrontier(X,
    spec |> add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
            add.objective(type = "risk", name = "StdDev"),
    type = "mean-StdDev", n.portfolios = n, optimize_method = "ROI")$frontier))
  grid <- seq(max(min(fr_es$mean), min(fr_sd$mean)),
              min(max(fr_es$mean), max(fr_sd$mean)), length.out = 40)
  at <- function(fr) stats::approx(fr$mean, fr$w.US_credit, xout = grid)$y
  gap <- at(fr_sd) - at(fr_es)                    # negative: the ES frontier holds more
  c(tail_obs = 0.05 * nrow(X),
    peak_variance_frontier = max(fr_sd$w.US_credit),
    peak_es_frontier = max(fr_es$w.US_credit),
    largest_gap = gap[which.max(abs(gap))])
}
ex2 <- rbind(monthly = credit_gap(Re, base_spec), weekly = credit_gap(Rew, spec_w))
round(ex2, 4)

# What changed between the two grids, for the series the gap is about: skewness,
# and expected shortfall per standard deviation with its rank among the sixteen.
tail_shape <- function(X) {
  es_sd <- apply(X, 2, function(x) loss_es(as.numeric(x)) / stats::sd(x))
  c(skewness = as.numeric(skewness(X[, "US_credit"])),
    ES_per_sd = es_sd[["US_credit"]], rank = rank(-es_sd)[["US_credit"]])
}
shape <- rbind(monthly = tail_shape(Re), weekly = tail_shape(Rew))

# The weeks that compound into the worst month, and the monthly variance against
# the weekly one scaled by the weeks in a month.
x_m   <- as.numeric(Re[, "US_credit"]); i <- which.min(x_m); d <- zoo::index(Re)
weeks <- as.numeric(Rew[zoo::index(Rew) > d[i - 1] & zoo::index(Rew) <= d[i], "US_credit"])
q     <- nrow(Rew) / nrow(Re)
var_ratio <- stats::var(x_m) / (q * stats::var(as.numeric(Rew[, "US_credit"])))
round(cbind(shape, weeks_in_worst_month = c(NA, length(weeks)), variance_ratio = c(NA, var_ratio)), 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex2-facts
#| include: false
# The orders the answer states; rows are monthly, then weekly.
stopifnot(identical(rownames(ex2), c("monthly", "weekly")), identical(rownames(shape), rownames(ex2)),
          all(ex2[, "largest_gap"] < 0), diff(abs(ex2[, "largest_gap"])) > 0,
          diff(ex2[, "peak_variance_frontier"]) > 0, diff(ex2[, "peak_es_frontier"]) > 0,
          ex2["weekly", "peak_es_frontier"] > ex2["weekly", "peak_variance_frontier"],
          in_episode(d[i], "credit_crisis"), all(weeks < 0), var_ratio > 1,
          diff(abs(shape[, "skewness"])) < 0, diff(shape[, "rank"]) > 0)
```

On the weekly grid the tail holds `r sprintf("%.0f", ex2["weekly", "tail_obs"])`
observations against `r sprintf("%.1f", ex2["monthly", "tail_obs"])`, and the
largest gap in the `US_credit` weight between the two frontiers widens,
from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * abs(ex2["monthly", "largest_gap"]))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * abs(ex2["weekly", "largest_gap"]))` percentage points, on
both grids with the expected-shortfall frontier holding more. Both peaks rise,
the variance frontier's from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ex2["monthly", "peak_variance_frontier"])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ex2["weekly", "peak_variance_frontier"])` and the
expected-shortfall frontier's from
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ex2["monthly", "peak_es_frontier"])` to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * ex2["weekly", "peak_es_frontier"])`. Four times as
many observations did not bring the two frontiers together, and they are not
observations of the same tail. The skewness of
`US_credit` is `r sprintf("%.2f", shape["monthly", "skewness"])` on the
monthly grid and `r sprintf("%.2f", shape["weekly", "skewness"])` on the
weekly one, because its worst month, `r fmt_model(d[i])` in the credit
crisis, is `r length(weeks)` consecutive weeks of losses that
compounding concentrates into one observation; and its weekly returns are
positively autocorrelated in the sense of @eq-03-lo, so that the monthly
variance is `r sprintf("%.2f", var_ratio)` times the weekly one scaled by the
`r sprintf("%.1f", q)` weeks in a month. Seen weekly, credit is less skewed
and, scaled to a month, less volatile, and its expected shortfall of
`r sprintf("%.2f", shape["weekly", "ES_per_sd"])` standard deviations ranks
`r shape["weekly", "rank"]` of the sixteen where the monthly one ranks
`r shape["monthly", "rank"]`: both measures buy more of it, and the
tail measure more than variance. Neither frontier was the noisier estimate of
the other's quantity: the horizon changed what there was to measure, and a tail
chosen at the weekly frequency says little about the tail an investor who
rebalances monthly will hold.

#### Exercise 3

The maximum-STARR portfolio can be read off the frontier by scanning, exactly
as chapter 9 read the tangency portfolio off the mean-variance frontier, or
requested through the default of a `mean` plus `ES` specification.

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex3
#| warning: false
spec_mean_es <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "ES", arguments = list(p = 0.95))
spec_mean_sd <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev")
fr_es <- as.data.frame(unclass(create.EfficientFrontier(Re, spec_mean_es, type = "mean-ETL",
                                                        n.portfolios = 100, optimize_method = "ROI")$frontier))
fr_sd <- as.data.frame(unclass(create.EfficientFrontier(Re, spec_mean_sd, type = "mean-StdDev",
                                                        n.portfolios = 100, optimize_method = "ROI")$frontier))
row_w <- function(fr, i) {
  wc <- grep("^w[.]", colnames(fr))
  setNames(as.numeric(fr[i, wc]), sub("^w[.]", "", colnames(fr)[wc]))[colnames(Re)]
}
w_starr_scan  <- row_w(fr_es, which.max(fr_es$mean / fr_es$ES))
w_starr_solve <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mean_es, optimize_method = "ROI"))  # maxSTARR = TRUE
w_tan         <- row_w(fr_sd, which.max(fr_sd$mean / fr_sd$StdDev))

mu <- colMeans(Re); S <- stats::cov(Re)
starr   <- function(w) { x <- as.numeric(Re %*% w); mean(x) / loss_es(x) }
p_vol   <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w)) * sqrt(12)
utility <- function(w, gamma = 4) 12 * (sum(mu * w) - gamma / 2 * as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w))
w_qu4 <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = 4 / 2), optimize_method = "ROI"))

cand <- list(`maximum STARR, scanned` = w_starr_scan, `maximum STARR, solved` = w_starr_solve,
             `tangency, scanned` = w_tan, `quadratic utility, gamma = 4` = w_qu4)
ex3 <- tibble::tibble(
  portfolio = names(cand),
  US_credit = vapply(cand, function(w) w[["US_credit"]], numeric(1)),
  vol       = vapply(cand, p_vol, numeric(1)),
  STARR     = vapply(cand, starr, numeric(1)),
  utility_gamma_4 = vapply(cand, utility, numeric(1)),
  from_solved = vapply(cand, function(w) sum(abs(w - w_starr_solve)) / 2, numeric(1)),
  from_gamma_4 = vapply(cand, function(w) sum(abs(w - w_qu4)) / 2, numeric(1))
)
ex3 |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 4))) |> as.data.frame()
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex3-facts
#| include: false
# The comparisons the answer makes, read by name rather than by row, and the
# two statements about `US_credit` asserted.
e3    <- function(p, col) ex3[[col]][ex3$portfolio == p]
ratio <- c(tangency = "tangency, scanned", `maximum-STARR` = "maximum STARR, solved")
ce    <- vapply(ratio, e3, numeric(1), col = "utility_gamma_4")
enter <- function(fr) min(fr$mean[fr$w.US_credit > 0.005])   # target at which the series is taken up
stopifnot(e3(ratio[["tangency"]], "US_credit") < 0.01, e3(ratio[["maximum-STARR"]], "US_credit") < 0.005,
          enter(fr_sd) < enter(fr_es))
```

The scanned and the solved maximum-STARR portfolios are
`r sprintf("%.3f", e3("maximum STARR, scanned", "from_solved"))` apart in turnover terms, the
discretization of a hundred-point frontier rather than a disagreement. The
tangency portfolio holds
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * e3(ratio[["tangency"]], "US_credit"))` in `US_credit` and the
tail-ratio portfolio
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * e3(ratio[["maximum-STARR"]], "US_credit"))`: both lie at
the low-return end of @fig-10-credit-weight, where the variance frontier has
just begun to take the series up and the expected-shortfall frontier has not.
Between the two ratio portfolios the investor of @eq-03-quadratic-utility with
$\gamma = 4$ prefers the `r names(which.max(ce))` portfolio,
at an annualized certainty equivalent of
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * max(ce))` against
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * min(ce))` for the `r names(which.min(ce))`
portfolio, and not because of any tail, which quadratic utility cannot see.
Both sit near the left end of the frontier, at volatilities of
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * e3(ratio[["maximum-STARR"]], "vol"))` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * e3(ratio[["tangency"]], "vol"))`, while that investor's own fully
invested optimum has `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * e3("quadratic utility, gamma = 4", "vol"))` and a certainty
equivalent of `r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * e3("quadratic utility, gamma = 4", "utility_gamma_4"))`; the preferred
ratio portfolio is simply the less bad of two portfolios that
sit `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * e3(ratio[["maximum-STARR"]], "from_gamma_4"))` and
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * e3(ratio[["tangency"]], "from_gamma_4"))` of the
portfolio away from what a $\gamma = 4$ investor holds under full investment.
That is the point of @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-application: a
ratio portfolio is the risky holding of an investor who can scale it against
the bill, not the choice of one who must be fully invested in it.

#### Exercise 4

Each search is seeded and given the same budget of about two thousand
objective evaluations; the linear program's portfolio is the benchmark,
evaluated on the modified measure it was not asked to minimize.

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex4
#| message: false
spec_mes <- base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES", arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "modified"))
w_es <- w_of(optimize.portfolio(Re, base_spec |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES", arguments = list(p = 0.95, method = "historical")),
  optimize_method = "ROI"))
mes_of <- function(w) {
  x <- as.numeric(Re %*% w); as.numeric(ES(x, p = 0.95, method = "modified", invert = FALSE))
}
set.seed(1602)
rp <- random_portfolios(base_spec, permutations = 2000, rp_method = "simplex")
search <- function(method, ...) {
  set.seed(1602)
  invisible(utils::capture.output(
    o <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_mes, optimize_method = method, ...)))
  mes_of(w_of(o))
}
ex4 <- tibble::tibble(
  route = c("random portfolios, simplex", "DEoptim, itermax = 25", "DEoptim, itermax = 100",
            "linear program, minimum historical ES"),
  modified_ES = c(search("random", rp = rp),
                  search("DEoptim", search_size = 2000, itermax = 25,  traceDE = 0),
                  search("DEoptim", search_size = 2000, itermax = 100, traceDE = 0),
                  mes_of(w_es))
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(relative_to_LP = modified_ES / modified_ES[route == "linear program, minimum historical ES"])
ex4 |> dplyr::mutate(modified_ES = round(modified_ES, 5), relative_to_LP = round(relative_to_LP, 3)) |>
  as.data.frame()
```

```{r}
#| label: sol-10-ex4-facts
#| include: false
searched <- ex4$relative_to_LP[ex4$route != "linear program, minimum historical ES"]
stopifnot(length(searched) == 3L, all(searched > 1))     # no search reaches the benchmark
```

None of the three searches reaches the modified expected shortfall of the
linear program's portfolio, which was chosen on a different measure: the best
of them lands
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (min(searched) - 1))` above it and
the worst `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (max(searched) - 1))`
above it. Because the objective is a smooth function of sixteen weights whose
minimum lies at a corner of the simplex, most of the population a
differential-evolution run spends its budget on is nowhere near that corner,
and a random-portfolio draw reaches it only by chance. This is the same
shortfall @sec-13-solvers-application reports on a problem with a known
answer, where the searches stop at a fraction of the attainable optimum; the
fraction here is of the same order once one recalls that the benchmark is
itself not the minimum of this objective, so the true gap is larger than the
table shows.
